Every quantity used by FCP-S is a function of the units. Each fold model is a symmetric function of the set of units it is trained on. Its training data are the whole families, which is allowed because a unit contains its entire family.
FCP-S is therefore exactly the K-fold CV+ procedure of Barber et al. (2021, Theorem 4) applied to G exchangeable data points Z_g, with the nonconformity score s(z; f) = |ỹ − μ_f(x̃)| / σ_f(x̃).
Barber et al.'s proof uses only two properties: the exchangeability of the data points (here, the units), and the inversion "y ∉ [μ − Rσ, μ + Rσ] ⟺ |y − μ|/σ > R", which holds for any σ > 0.

runs.t: What is and is not covered.

items.t: FCP-W replaces the single random draw per family by its expectation: every alloy of family g receives weight 1/n_g, so each family carries unit mass. This is the pooled-CDF construction of Dunn et al. (2023). It removes the variance of the random draw, but the proposition does not literally apply to it.
The unweighted FCP gives large families proportionally more weight. It targets alloy-level coverage and is not covered by Proposition 1 either. Both are evaluated empirically in the main text.
FCP-S itself is implemented (`calibration_weights(..., "subsample")` in `code/src/fcp/models/conformal.py`, stage `fcps`) and evaluated in Section 9.6 of the main text.

runs.t: The weighted quantile in Eq. (8) is finite only if G/(G+1) ≥ 1 − α (Eq. 10). For α = 0.1 this requires G ≥ 9 training families.

If calibration alloys are drawn at random, a calibration alloy usually shares its family with training alloys, while the test alloy does not. The calibration residuals are then not exchangeable with the test residual, and no guarantee of the above kind holds. Barber et al. (2023) bound the resulting coverage loss by the total-variation distance between the two score distributions, which can be large under family shift. Section 7 shows that it is large in practice.
Barber et al.'s K-fold result assumes K folds of exactly G/K points. The implementation assigns whole families to folds so that the folds hold similar numbers of

, so the number of families per fold varies somewhat. The bound is then an approximation for the implemented procedure; assigning families in round-robin order would satisfy the assumption exactly (with G divisible by K).

With G = 100 training families and K = 5 folds, the correction term is min{2(0.8)/21, 0.95/6} ≈ 0.076. The guarantee at α = 0.1 is then about 0.72, conservative as is typical for CV+. Empirically, CV+ and FCP cover close to 1 − α (Section 7).

runs.t: The study concerns regression intervals, so classification diagnostics (confusion matrices, ROC and PR curves) do not apply. Their roles are taken by coverage-versus-nominal plots (Fig. S1), conditional coverage by novelty (main-text Fig. 7), parity plots with intervals (Fig. S4) and per-family error analysis (main-text Fig. 9). Tree ensembles are not trained iteratively with a validation loss, so training curves are not shown. Hyper-parameter sensitivity is reported instead (Fig. S2).
